questions.question: When will quantum computers actually be useful?

hybrid.answer:
Quantum computers start being useful with the first provable quantum advantage, which at IBM we expect in 2026, and the transformational impact comes by 2030 with the first fault-tolerant machine.

**First advantage (2026):** At IBM we expect real advantage from a quantum application on a real system that classical computing alone can't do [1]. The later talk puts it as a provable, closed quantum advantage on some application by the following year [2]. Early results are already appearing, such as HSBC getting 34% better accuracy in predicting whether a stock order gets filled at a given price, though I noted there's no proof yet that a classical computer couldn't do it [3].

**Transformational impact (by 2030):** By 2030 we expect the first fault-tolerant quantum computer, a machine implementing universal quantum computing [2]. That is where the real transformational power arrives, within this decade [1].

**Useful already, in limited ways:** Today we can already simulate small molecules, and even without full error correction the scaling is a slower exponential, so you can get value now [4].

**Why I trust this timeline:** A technology is real if it has a roadmap, and at IBM we have not missed a point on ours since 2016 [5].

**Where it will matter most:** Simulating nature (atoms, molecules, proteins), global optimization, and finding structure in small but complex datasets [6][7].

questions.question: Should banks be worried about quantum computers breaking encryption?

hybrid.answer:
Yes. Banks should act now, because the risk is already present and I think we are already late [1].

**Why it matters:** At IBM, our roadmap points to the first fault-tolerant quantum computing machine by 2030 [2]. At that point, the asymmetric (public-key) cryptography that secures internet connections, digital signatures and data transmission will be attacked and no longer work [3]. That also covers secure digital currency, such as a digital euro in the future [3].

**Why waiting is a mistake:** Someone is already collecting encrypted data circulating on the internet and storing it. Once the capability exists, they can go back, read it, and even forge digital signatures and contracts [4]. So it's wrong to assume that breaking this will only be possible in 30 years [1].

**What to do:** Solutions exist to move from today's cryptography to something secure against quantum attacks, but one has to start now [1]. I'd also build in crypto agility, so you can migrate easily from one cryptography to another. Nobody can guarantee the new quantum-safe algorithms will stay secure forever, since cryptography by definition isn't secure forever [5].

questions.question: What about the energy cost of all this AI?

hybrid.answer:
I think the energy cost is a real issue, and the way to handle it is to build many specialized models rather than one giant one.

**The single giant model.** One model that integrates all data and modalities could bring many discoveries [1]. But it is hugely expensive, especially in use, because training happens once while use happens a million times [1]. Using a model with 1,000 trillion parameters to decide where to go for dinner makes no sense [2]. Training energy also doesn't scale linearly with model size, but at least quadratically [3].

**The better way.** Build many models of around 1 to 10 trillion parameters, each specialized in a task, modality or use case, with an orchestrator on top. The orchestrator can itself be an AI model, which is what people call agentic AI [4]. Done right, this can use an order of magnitude less energy and also be more accurate [5].

**Avoiding duplicated effort.** I push for base models to be built once, openly and collaboratively, in a pre-competitive way. Otherwise people redo the same models with a lot of compute and CO2 emissions to reach the same result [6].

questions.question: What does he think about Bitcoin?

hybrid.answer: I haven't covered Bitcoin in my videos yet. The closest thing I've said is that once quantum computers reach fault tolerance, public-key cryptography will be attacked and stop working. That includes the cryptography behind secure digital currency such as a future digital euro [1]. I also said we're already late in moving to quantum-safe solutions, and that crypto agility, the ability to migrate easily from one cryptography to another, is worth building [2][3].
